extracted.intended_audience: writers, literature students, narratology scholars, and general readers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Theory, classification, and signals for identifying or creating unreliable narrators in literature and film; covers definitions, typologies, theoretical models, and textual signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'unreliable narrator'
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator is a narrator who cannot be trusted, one whose credibility is compromised. While almost by definition first-person, arguments have been made for unreliable second- and third-person narrators (especially in film and television).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the baseline criterion: credibility (trustworthiness) of the narrator is the central issue. Note the device appears across ages and ages of characters; consider mode (literature, film) when applying the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate vs. delayed revelation of unreliability (use and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the narrator's unreliability is made immediately evident (e.g., opening with a plainly false or delusional claim or admitting severe mental illness, or via a frame that reveals the narrator as a character). A more dramatic use delays the revelation until near the story's end (a twist ending), forcing readers to reconsider their point of view. In some cases the unreliability is only hinted at and never fully revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing of revelation as a design choice: immediate signals set reader expectations; delayed revelation creates twist/reinterpretation; partial hints invite sustained reader uncertainty. Use framing to control when and how credibility is undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riggan: The Pícaro
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narrator of a picaresque novel; an antihero whose behavior is marked by rebelliousness, resentment, and aggression with a worldview characterized by resignation and pessimism. There is a gap between the pícaro's entertaining account and his self-indulgent explanations and morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Apuleius (The Golden Ass), Lázaro (Lazarillo de Tormes), Moll (Moll Flanders). Use when the narrator's charm and self-justification mask a moral or perceptual gap that readers detect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riggan: The Clown
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator in the tradition of the fool/court jester whose unreliable narration includes irony, variations of meaning, ambiguities, and possibilities for reversals and counter-reversals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Folly (In Praise of Folly), Tristram Shandy, Humbert Humbert (Lolita), Oskar Matzerath (The Tin Drum). Employ irony and playfulness; reader must negotiate multiple possible readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riggan: The Madman
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator untrustworthy due to an 'unbalanced mind'—traits include being petty, withdrawn, defensive, dreaming, spiteful, perversely logical, self-deluding; often perceived immediately as of questionable trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Poprishchin (Diary of a Madman), narrator of Notes from Underground, Poe's first-person narrators. Signal unreliability via clear markers of psychopathology or distorted perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riggan: The Naïf
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose nature is revealed through their narration without their conscious awareness; lacks experience to handle moral, ethical, emotional, and intellectual questions arising from their account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Huckleberry Finn, Holden Caulfield. Unreliability arises from limited knowledge or maturity rather than deceit—readers infer gaps between narrator's perception and fuller reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Booth's norm-conformity criterion (reliable vs. unreliable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator is 'reliable' when he speaks for or acts in accordance with the norms of the work (the implied author's norms), and 'unreliable' when he does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conformity to implied-authorial norms as an analytic test, but be aware critiques that this relies on external value judgments and the contested notion of the 'implied author.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rabinowitz's audience-based redefinition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabinowitz argues against Booth's reliance on external norms and reframes unreliability with attention to types of audiences: actual audience (real readers), authorial audience (hypothetical audience author addresses), narrative audience (imitation audience with particular knowledge), and ideal narrative audience (uncritical audience). He emphasizes that an unreliable narrator is one who tells lies, conceals information, or misjudges relative to the narrative audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess statements against what the narrative audience would accept as true; consider the distinctions among audience types when judging truthfulness and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nünning's cognitive/signals approach to unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliability can be reconceptualized through frame theory and readers' cognitive strategies: it depends on definable signals (textual data plus reader's preexisting world-knowledge). Whether a narrator is unreliable depends on the distance between the narrator's view of the world and the reader's world-model and standards of normality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor identifiable textual signals over purely intuitive judgments; evaluate discrepancies between narrator assertions and other textual cues or reader knowledge. This frames unreliability as a reader strategy of reconciling discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals of unreliable narration — intratextual signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Intratextual signs include the narrator contradicting themselves, having gaps in memory, or lying to other characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for textual contradictions, omissions, memory lapses, or direct deceptions within the narrative as strong evidence of unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals of unreliable narration — extratextual signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Extratextual signs involve the narrator contradicting the reader's general world knowledge or presenting impossibilities (within the parameters of logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare narrator claims to external commonsense knowledge or logical consistency; impossible events or blatant factual errors are extratextual markers of unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals of unreliable narration — reader's literary competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' knowledge about literary types (stock characters), genre conventions, and stylistic devices contributes to perceiving unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genre expectations and familiarity with tropes to detect when a narrator is performing (e.g., picaresque boasting) or omitting information; reader competence is part of the signal set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olson's fallibility vs. untrustworthiness spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: All fictional texts using unreliability can be considered along a spectrum from trustworthiness to unreliability, allowing for shades of grey between fallibility and untrustworthiness; different readers will place narrators differently on this scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reliability as a continuum rather than a binary; distinguish between 'fallible' (honest mistakes, limited knowledge) and 'untrustworthy' (deceitful or manipulative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of unreliable non‑first‑person narration (restricted information)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate restriction of information to the audience can create instances of unreliable narrative even if not an 'unreliable narrator' strictly speaking; multiple perspectives (e.g., Rashomon effect) or restricted focalization can produce unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or designing unreliability, consider focalization and information control: an ostensibly objective third-person can still mislead readers by restricting access to facts or perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phelan's 'bonding unreliability' (ethical/affective function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phelan coins 'bonding unreliability' to describe situations where unreliable narration ultimately serves to bring the narrator closer to the work's envisioned audience, creating a bonding communication between the implied author and the authorial audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider unreliability's rhetorical/ethical effects: it can distance or—paradoxically—create intimacy and complicity between narrator and reader; assess intended audience alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing devices and narrative techniques that enable or signal unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame stories, plays within plays, tall tales, the Rashomon effect, and other devices can be used to present or highlight unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing unreliable narration, use frames and devices purposefully to contextualize the narrator's credibility or to provide alternative perspectives that reveal contradictions.
